descriptionChirho: The virtue or disposition of thinking modestly about oneself and placing others' interests above one's own; a key Pauline and Petrine ethical term used for the foundational Christian virtue of self-lowering service (Phil 2:3, Col 2:18, 2:23, 3:12; Eph 4:2; Acts 20:19; 1 Pet 5:5). Spanish 'humildad/humillación' (humility/humiliation) captures both the virtue and its experiential cost; Hindi 'नम्रत' (gentleness, humility) and 'दिखवति-नम्रत' (showy humility, i.e., false humility in Col 2:18-23) reveal the important theological distinction between genuine and pretended humility; Arabic 'تَواضُع' (humility, modesty) from the root w-ḍ-ʿ (to be low); Korean '겸손' (謙遜, modesty/humility) uses Sino-Korean characters emphasizing self-deprecation; Swahili 'unyenyekevu' (humility, meekness) is the abstract noun form of the humble disposition.

labelChirho: humble-minded, having a disposition of humility (adjectival)
descriptionChirho: Used adjectivally to describe persons who embody the quality of humility in their thinking and comportment; in 1 Peter 3:8 as a summary ethical exhortation to be 'humble-minded' alongside being compassionate and sympathetic. This adjectival usage differs from the abstract noun sense by describing the persons themselves rather than the virtue as a concept. Spanish 'humildes' (humble ones) shifts to describing people; Hindi 'नम्रचित्त' (namra-chitta, gentle-minded) is a compound explicitly joining humility with the mind/heart, showing the dispositional character; Arabic 'مُتَواضِعين' (humble ones) uses the active participle form denoting people characterized by humility; Korean '겸손하라' (be humble — imperative form) captures the exhortative context of 1 Peter 3:8; Swahili 'wanyenyekevu' (humble people) uses the animate plural class prefix.
